title: US Suspends Microsoft, Adobe and Six IT Firms From Green Card Program
excerpt: Vice President JD Vance announced the PERM suspension at the White House, accusing the firms of replacing laid-off Americans with foreign workers; thousands of Indians in green-card backlogs face fresh uncertainty.
body:
• The United States has suspended Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini from the Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) program — the mandatory first step for most employment-based green cards.
  • Announced Thursday at the White House by Vice President JD Vance alongside Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling, the suspension halts all new and pending PERM applications involving the named firms, effective immediately, with no end date given.
  • The administration accused the firms of fraud and abuse: Microsoft laid off 6,000 U.S. workers in 2025 while filing 3,682 PERM applications, including nearly 1,000 for the same positions as the laid-off workers, according to the administration.
  • What it means for you: thousands of Indian professionals at these firms — many stuck in decade-long green-card backlogs — can no longer advance their status through their employer, leaving them tied to their current jobs and exposed to visa-renewal hurdles.

The United States on Thursday suspended eight major technology firms — Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini — from the Permanent Labor Certification program, the government pipeline through which most skilled foreign workers obtain green cards. The announcement, made at the White House by Vice President JD Vance, is the most aggressive move yet in the administration's crackdown on employment-based immigration.

What the White House announced

Vance announced the suspension alongside Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling, Attorney General Todd Blanche, White House deputy chief of staff and homeland security adviser Stephen Miller, and Labor Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito, framing it as an action of his government fraud task force, according to Reuters and the Associated Press.

https://x.com/Resonant_News/status/2108226946375225648

The mechanism is the PERM program, run by the Department of Labor. Under it, an employer must obtain federal certification that no qualified, willing and available American worker exists for a specific job — a required step before most employment-based green card petitions can proceed. Sonderling was blunt about the scope: "We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labor certification applications involving these companies."

Vance put the intended effect in plainer terms: "They'll no longer be able to take those H-1Bs and apply for permanent resident status within the United States of America."

The firms and the numbers

Sonderling named the targets directly: "I am hereby suspending from the Permanent Labour Certification Programme some of the largest IT outsourcing firms in the world, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini." Microsoft and Adobe were suspended alongside them.

Microsoft drew the sharpest fire. The administration said the company laid off 6,000 U.S. workers in 2025 while certifying that it could not find qualified Americans — and was approved for more than 6,000 H-1B visas while filing 3,682 PERM applications, including nearly 1,000 for the same positions as the laid-off workers. Vance did not hold back: "If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants." He added: "There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused this system more than Microsoft." Microsoft did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

"If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants."

— JD Vance, Vice President of the United States

The outsourcing firms were measured on a longer ledger. "Since 2009, just these companies alone have requested almost 3 million foreign workers. They've received over 230,000 H-1B visa approvals and over 100,000 permanent labour certifications," Sonderling said.

There was an earlier warning sign few noticed. PERM Tracker data from September 26 showed 215 of Adobe's 215 pending PERM cases — and 1,831 of Cognizant's 1,831 — listed as "application on hold," with 2,070 cases on hold nationwide as of September 25. At the time, the reason was unclear.

What happens to pending applicants

The administration did not specify how long the suspension will last or the precise handling of pending cases — only that pending applications will not be processed and new ones will not be accepted. For the thousands of Indian professionals at the named firms, the effect is immediate: those in long green-card backlogs cannot advance their status through their employer, leaving them tied indefinitely to their current jobs and vulnerable to visa-renewal hurdles.

The wider crackdown

The PERM suspension is part of a broader offensive. Vance said nine universities — including Harvard, Yale and Stanford — would be investigated for allegedly bringing in international students on J-1 visas to undercut American wages, and the Labor Inspector General said subpoenas had already been served. "If an American university is breaking the law to save $1 while exposing American research to a foreign adversary, that is not academic excellence. It's institutional betrayal," D'Esposito said.

The announcement came a day after the Department of Homeland Security proposed a $70,000 fee on educational institutions for a student's first participation in Optional Practical Training — $30,000 for renewals — and as the administration's H-1B fee faces another court challenge. It also landed hours before President Trump was scheduled to award the National Medal of Technology and Innovation to Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella.

"If an American university is breaking the law to save $1 while exposing American research to a foreign adversary, that is not academic excellence. It's institutional betrayal."

— Anthony D'Esposito, Labor Department Inspector General

What comes next

No legal challenge had been reported as of Thursday evening, but the companies have strong incentives to sue — and immigration lawyers will be watching for Labor Department guidance on how pending cases are treated. For Indian H-1B holders, the practical question is whether the suspension is a negotiating tactic or the new normal. Either way, the green-card pipeline through America's largest IT employers just narrowed dramatically.
